text: Nuclear power plant structures and components are designed so that the working stress under various operational loading conditions does not exceed the yield or ultimate tensile strength of materials in general. In the engineering evaluation to ensure the structural integrity of structures and components, therefore, an elastic analysis is performed assuming that stresses are linearly proportional to strains. This is an excessively conservative method that does not take into account strain hardening even though plastic deformation occurs signi fi cantly in actual materials under some large loading conditions.

text: Knowing a material ' s true stress-strain curve is essential for performing a nonlinear fi nite element analysis to solve an elastoplastic problem. This study presents a simple methodology to determine the true stress-strain curve of type 304 and 316 austenitic stainless steels in the full range of strain from a typical tensile test. Before necking, the true stress and strain values are directly converted from engineering stress and strain data, respectively. After necking, a true stress-strain equation is determined by iteratively conducting fi nite element analysis using three pieces of information at the necking and the fracture points. The Hockett-Sherby equation is proposed as an optimal stress-strain model in a nonuniform deformation region. The application to the stainless steel under different temperatures and loading conditions veri fi es that the strain hardening behavior of the material is adequately described by the determined equation, and the estimated engineering stress-strain curves are in good agreement with those of experiments. The presented method is intrinsically simple to use and reduces iterations because it does not require much experimental effort and adopts the approach of determining the stress-strain equation instead of correcting the individual stress at each strain point.

text: The true stress-strain relationship in the region of uniform deformation may be identi fi ed through typical tensile testing. Such testing involves a method of simply converting the engineering stress-strain values, where necking does not yet occur, to the true stress-strain ones, and then fi tting them using an appropriate equation [5 e 7]. To identify the stress-strain relation in a nonuniform deformation region as well as in a uniform deformation region, there are methods of fi tting the true stress-strain data in the uniform deformation region and then extending the fi tted curve to the non-uniform deformation region [8 e 12]. In References [5 e 12], the stress-strain models for fi tting adopt a power law form of equations such as Hollomon ' s [13], Swift ' s [14], and Ludwik ' s [15], an exponential form of equations such as Voce ' s [16] and HockettSherby ' s [17], or a combination of them.

text: A direct method for obtaining the true stress-strain data after necking is to continuously measure the shape of the test specimen [17 e 20]. Hockett et al. proposed a more generalized equation by modifying Voce ' s equation, which describes the true stress-strain relation in a large strain region through compression tests on alpha uranium, pure iron, and 1100 aluminum [17,18]. Using a digital image correlation technique, the real-time measurement and analysis of the deformation shape of a specimen have been applied to obtain the true stress-strain data in the full range of strain [19,20]. In order to accurately identify the plastic fl ow characteristics after necking, there have been methods of acquiring the true stress-strain data through the consecutive measurement of the specimen deformation shape and iteratively correcting the true stress-strain data by performing fi nite element analysis [21 e 24]. These are methods to directly acquire the true stress-strain data in the full range of strain by measuring the specimen deformation shape. In particular, more reliable results are expected by performing a fi nite element analysis in conjunction with measurement. There are, however, dif fi culties in accurately measuring the deformation shape of a specimen because of the need for specialist equipment.

text: Many methods using a fi nite element analysis without special measurements after necking have been introduced to obtain the true stress-strain data over the entire strain range [25 e 32]. After assuming the initial true stress-strain curve from existing equations, studies have iteratively corrected the true stress-strain data in the non-uniform deformation region using the difference of the engineering stress values at each strain point between the experiment and the fi nite element analysis. However, the number of iterations may be intrinsically high due to the one-by-one corrections at each strain point, and the stress-strain equation of the fi nal true stress-strain curve after completing corrections was not presented for corresponding material.

text: Austenitic stainless steel such as type 304 or 316 is widely used in nuclear power plants because of its strong corrosion resistance, excellent welding performance, high strength, and other advantageous characteristics. Although some research has been published regarding the stress-strain relationship of stainless steel, that research only deals with the uniform deformation [7,33,34], or the mathematical models presented in relation to the non-uniform deformation are not con fi rmed by experimental results [35,36]. The method correcting point-by-point the true stress-strain data in the range of non-uniform deformation by the use of fi nite element analysis has been introduced for stainless steel [24,32]. However, the operating temperatures and strain rates in nuclear power plants where stainless steel is used were not taken into account.

text: This paper presents a simple method to determine the true stress-strain curve of type 304 and 316 austenitic stainless steels in the full range of strain without continuous measurement of the specimen deformation shape in typical tensile testing. The tensile stress fl ow and strain hardening behavior of materials are investigated in the post-necking region. A stress-strain model that re fl ects the deformation behavior of type 304 and 316 stainless steels is proposed, and the equations pertaining to the model are fi nally determined by comparing the engineering stress-strain curve predicted from fi nite element analysis with that of experiment, and iteratively correcting it.

text: For the prediction of the fl ow stress of a specimen subjected to tensile loading, there are two distinct parts of strain hardening behavior, the before and after necking stages. The fi rst part includes the data before the onset of the necking, whereas the second part involves the continuation of the stress-strain curve from the necking to the fracture. Since a specimen is uniformly deformed as a whole before necking, it is placed in a uniaxial stress state. After the necking onset, however, a specimen central region is nonuniformly deformed and placed in a multiaxial stress state. The stress and strain are no longer uniformly distributed along the specimen at high levels of elongation due to the necking formation; therefore, the engineering stress-strain curve cannot provide proper information of the physical phenomena of the specimen involved in the test. In general, it is dif fi cult to accurately describe both stages with one stress-strain model on account of the inherently different deformation behavior.

text: Several models between stress and strain have been widely used to describe plastic stress fl ow and strain hardening behavior. The most commonly used equations of the models, for instance, Hollomon, Ludwik, and Swift, are the power law forms of Eqs. (7) e (9), respectively. These equations, which have been developed with a fundamentally different approach, have a distinct feature with asymptotic stress value after severe deformation.
